slides.title: What is a Meeting?
text: What is a Meeting?
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
A purposeful gathering to discuss, coordinate, and accomplish shared objectives.
Definition
A meeting is a structured conversation where people come together to share information, make decisions, and coordinate action.
Meetings are the primary communication mechanism in every IT team — from daily standups to board-level strategic reviews.
What makes a meeting effective?
▪ Clear purpose and agenda ▪ Right people in the room ▪ Documented outcomes (minutes) ▪ Action items with owners & deadlines
Why Meetings Matter for IT Professionals
🗂 Align teams — on sprint goals, project scope, and technical decisions
🤝 Build relationships — with clients, stakeholders, and cross-functional teams
🔍 Solve problems — collaboratively and make decisions with full context
📣 Communicate progress — and blockers to management and peers
🚀 Drive careers — by demonstrating leadership, communication, and initiative

slides.title: Formal vs. Informal Meetings
text: Formal vs. Informal Meetings
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Both types are common in IT workplaces — knowing the difference shapes how you prepare.
FORMAL
Pre-planned with structured agenda, chairperson, formal notice, and written minutes.
When to use:
Strategic decisions, stakeholder reviews, board meetings, project sign-offs
Examples:
Board meetings, AGMs, sprint reviews, client requirement sessions, EGMs
INFORMAL
Less structured — no required agenda, chairperson, or minutes. Direction can shift.
When to use:
Quick problem-solving, information sharing, team alignment, brainstorming
Examples:
Daily standups, pair-programming sessions, hallway chats, team check-ins
VIRTUAL
Any formal or informal meeting conducted via Zoom, MS Teams, Google Meet.
When to use:
Distributed teams, remote work, cross-timezone collaboration
Examples:
Remote standups, client demos, online interviews, hybrid team meetings

slides.title: Meetings Across Development Methodologies
text: Meetings Across Development Methodologies
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Different methodologies = different meeting cadences — both require structured communication.
🏗 Waterfall
Sequential phases — meetings concentrated at phase gates
Requirements
Stakeholder meetings to gather and sign off on requirements
Design
Architecture review meetings — design decisions documented
Implementation
Progress check-ins, issue resolution meetings
Testing
QA review meetings, defect triage sessions
Deployment
Go/no-go meetings, post-launch retrospectives
🔄 Agile / Scrum
Iterative sprints — meetings are continuous ceremonies
Sprint Planning
Define goals and assign backlog items for the sprint
Daily Standup
15-min: What did I do? What will I do? Any blockers?
Sprint Review
Demo completed features to stakeholders — get feedback
Retrospective
What went well? What to improve? Action items for next sprint
Backlog Refinement
Estimate, clarify, and prioritise upcoming work items

slides.title: Why Discussion Methods Matter in Meeting
text: Why Discussion Methods Matter in Meeting
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Not every meeting needs the same voice.
Effective IT professionals choose discussion methods intentionally — matching the technique to what the meeting actually needs to achieve.
The wrong method wastes time. The right one accelerates decisions, surfaces hidden concerns, and distributes voice fairly across the team.
Before choosing a discussion method, ask:
What outcome do we need?
Are you generating ideas, making a decision, surfacing concerns, or assigning ownership? Each requires a different structure.
Who needs to contribute?
Some methods favour vocal participants. Others — like go-around or spend-a-dollar — ensure quieter team members have equal weight.
How much time do we have?
Brainstorming is open-ended. List-and-commit is fast and closure-focused. Matching method to time budget keeps meetings productive.

slides.title: Discussion methods
text: Discussion methods
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Go-around: Taking turns in a circle
Feedback: Responding to specific questions about an idea
Share info and needs: Presenting information and requesting support
Spend-a-dollar: Ranking priorities by allocating 100 cents across options
Brainstorm: Generating ideas freely without evaluation
List items and get commitment: Capturing action items with clear ownership

slides.title: Meeting Minutes — Purpose & Process
text: Meeting Minutes — Purpose & Process
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Minutes transform conversation into accountability. Without them, you have no recourse.
What minutes must capture
📌 What was decided
Decisions, resolutions, outcomes agreed by the group
✅ What needs to be done
Action items — specific tasks with clear owners
📅 By when
Deadlines for every action item — no ambiguity
⚠ Without minutes, you may need to repeat the entire meeting if actions aren't completed.
Minutes creation process
Pre-planning Use the agenda as your minutes template — start before the meeting
Record-taking Clarify expected level of detail with chair before starting
Writing Capture decisions, accomplishments, and all future actions
Sharing Distribute within 24 hours via email, Teams, or Google Drive
Storage File in accessible location for future reference and accountability

slides.title: Using Microsoft Copilot — Assignment 1 Group Research Meeting
text: Using Microsoft Copilot — Assignment 1 Group Research Meeting
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Scenario: Your 4-person team is meeting to coordinate the Assignment 1 report on ChatGPT ethics in healthcare.
📋 Team: Aisha (Team Lead), Ben (Researcher), Chloe (Writer), Dev (Reviewer) | 📌 Goal: Coordinate research tasks, agree on sources, assign report sections, confirm submission plan.
STEP 1 · Draft the Kickoff Meeting Agenda

Objective: Draft a 60-minute agenda for a 4-person student research group meeting. The team is planning an IT ethics report on ChatGPT use in healthcare. Output format: Table — Item, Desired Outcome, Owner, Time, Discussion Method. Include: opening check-in, source assignment, search strategy review, section allocation, deadline setting, and closing actions.
STEP 2 · Generate Meeting Minutes

Objective: From these rough notes [paste notes from your team meeting], create formal minutes for a student research group planning session. Output format: Sections — Date/Attendees, Decisions Made, Action Items (Owner + Deadline), Outstanding Issues, Next Meeting. Keep it concise and professional.
STEP 3 · Verify, Attribute & Declare AI Use

✔ Check accuracy: Confirm all names, section owners, and deadlines are correct before sharing with your team. ✔ Declare AI use: Note in your minutes that Copilot assisted drafting — required for academic integrity. ⚠ Never submit AI-generated meeting records as-is — you are responsible for accuracy.

slides.title: AI Features in Video Conferencing Platforms
text: AI Features in Video Conferencing Platforms
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Zoom and Microsoft Teams include built-in AI tools — use them to run better meetings.
🎥 Zoom — AI Companion
▸ Meeting Summary: Auto-generates summary with action items after every meeting
▸ Live Transcription: Real-time captions and searchable transcript
▸ Smart Recording: Highlights, chapters, and searchable meeting moments
▸ Ask AI Companion: Ask questions about past meetings: 'What did we decide on X?'
▸ Whiteboard AI: Generate diagrams and frameworks from text prompts
💬 Google Meet — Gemini
▸ Meeting Transcript: Auto-generates a full searchable transcript — saved to Google Docs
▸ Gemini Summaries: Produces a written summary of key discussion points and decisions after the call
▸ Smart Nudge: Prompts late joiners with a catch-up summary: 'Here is what you missed'
▸ Take Notes for Me: Gemini takes structured notes in a linked Google Doc in real time
▸ Ask Gemini: Ask questions about the meeting after it ends: 'What action items were assigned?'

slides.title: The STAR Technique — Structured Communication
text: The STAR Technique — Structured Communication
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
A framework for presenting experiences clearly in meetings, interviews, performance reviews, and cover letters.
S
Situation
Set the scene — describe the context and background so your audience understands the circumstances.
T
Task
State your specific responsibility — what were you asked or required to do?
A
Action
Explain the steps you personally took — focus on your contribution, not the team's.
R
Result
Describe the outcome — ideally quantified. What changed because of your actions?
T

slides.title: STAR in Action — Software Bug Scenario
text: STAR in Action — Software Bug Scenario
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
Behavioural question: "Tell me about a time you solved a critical problem under pressure."
S

Situation: During my final-year project, we discovered a critical authentication bug 48 hours before our beta launch to 200 test users. The bug exposed user session tokens and could have caused a full security breach.
T
Task: As the security lead on the team, I was responsible for identifying the root cause, coordinating the fix, and ensuring we met the launch deadline without compromising user safety.
A

Action: I called an emergency standup, assigned debugging tasks based on team expertise, implemented a temporary session invalidation patch within 4 hours, and documented the vulnerability for our final report.
R
Result: We launched on time with zero security incidents. The client gave us the highest feedback rating in the cohort. The patch approach was later adopted as a standard process by our supervisor.

slides.title: STAR — When to Use & Best Practices
text: STAR — When to Use & Best Practices
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4
STAR works beyond interviews — it is a general professional communication framework.
When to use STAR
💼 Job interviews — Behavioural questions: 'Tell me about a time…'
📋 Performance reviews — Demonstrate impact with evidence
📝 Cover letters — Structure your 'experience' paragraph
🗣 Meeting updates — Report on progress with clear outcomes
🤝 Client presentations — Show your problem-solving credibility
🎓 Assessment tasks — FIT1055 oral presentations and reflections
Tips for effective STAR responses
✦ Keep it concise — aim for 90–120 seconds verbally
✦ Use a conversational tone — avoid sounding rehearsed
✦ Quantify results where possible (%, time saved, users impacted)
✦ Focus on YOUR specific contribution — not the team's
✦ Choose examples that highlight skills relevant to the role
✦ Prepare 3–4 strong examples that can flex across question types
✦ Anticipate follow-up questions: 'What would you do differently?'

slides.title: Summary: Week 4 Key Takeaways
text: Summary: Week 4 Key Takeaways
FIT1055: IT Professional Practice and Ethics | Week 4

✔ Meetings are critical communication structures in IT — formal meetings follow structured agendas and produce written minutes; informal meetings enable rapid, flexible collaboration ✔ Waterfall concentrates meetings at phase gates; Agile/Scrum uses continuous ceremonies (standups, planning, review, retrospective) — both require structured communication ✔ Effective agendas define Item, Outcome, Priority, Time, Owner, and Discussion Method — minutes must capture what was decided, what must be done, and by when ✔ Copilot can draft agendas and minutes — always verify accuracy, declare AI use, and never distribute unreviewed output ✔ Zoom and Google Meet include AI transcription, summaries, and action item extraction — leverage these tools to increase meeting productivity ✔ STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) structures responses in interviews, performance reviews, cover letters, and professional meetings
